values.label: Oxygen's share of the air breathed in (atmospheric air)
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, Table 22.2 Partial Pressures of Atmospheric Gases (columns: percent of total composition, partial pressure in mm Hg): “Oxygen (O 2 ) 20.9 158.8”
values.note: The source gives a single value, not a range. Supplemental oxygen raises this share in the model.

values.label: Oxygen partial pressure in the air breathed in (atmospheric air)
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, Table 22.2 Partial Pressures of Atmospheric Gases (columns: percent of total composition, partial pressure in mm Hg): “Oxygen (O 2 ) 20.9 158.8”
values.note: The source gives a single value for dry atmospheric air, not a range. The model uses it as the air reaching the alveoli and leaves out humidification.

values.label: Oxygen partial pressure in the alveoli
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, Ventilation and Perfusion: “The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is about 104 mm Hg”
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range. The model prints the average over its two air sacs, weighted by how much air each receives.

values.label: Carbon dioxide partial pressure in the alveoli
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, External Respiration: “The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood of the capillary is about 45 mm Hg, whereas its partial pressure in the alveoli is about 40 mm Hg.”
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range. Weighted by air, as for alveolar oxygen.

values.label: Oxygen partial pressure in blood arriving at the lung capillaries
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, External Respiration: “The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is about 104 mm Hg, whereas its partial pressure in the blood of the capillary is about 40 mm Hg.”
values.note: A fixed input of the model: blood always arrives with this oxygen pressure.

values.label: Carbon dioxide partial pressure in blood arriving at the lung capillaries
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, External Respiration: “The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood of the capillary is about 45 mm Hg, whereas its partial pressure in the alveoli is about 40 mm Hg.”
values.note: A fixed input of the model.

values.label: Oxygen partial pressure in blood leaving the lungs (pulmonary veins)
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, Ventilation and Perfusion: “The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is about 104 mm Hg, whereas the partial pressure of oxygenated blood in pulmonary veins is about 100 mm Hg.”
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range. The model's healthy baseline is tuned to land on it.

values.label: Hemoglobin saturation
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.5 Transport of Gases, Function of Hemoglobin: “In a healthy individual with normal hemoglobin levels, hemoglobin saturation generally ranges from 95 percent to 99 percent.”
values.note: The model's marker is the saturation of the mixed blood leaving its lungs. This bar starts at 50 so small changes show.

values.label: Ventilation–perfusion ratio, whole lung
values.where: StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK526127, Respiratory Failure in Adults, Pathophysiology, Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch: “In healthy subjects, however, the V/Q ratio is approximately 0.8, as the balance between ventilation and perfusion differs from the apex to the base of the lungs.”
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range. The model's marker is all the air it moves divided by all the blood it moves.

values.label: Ventilation–perfusion ratio in one region of the lung
values.where: StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK539907, Physiology, Pulmonary Ventilation and Perfusion, Mechanism: “In a healthy individual, the V/Q ratio is 1 at the middle of the lung, with a minimal spread of V/Q ratios from 0.3 to 2.1 from base to apex.”
values.note: The band is the healthy spread from the base to the top of the lung. The model's marker is its right-hand air sac, the region each disease in this lesson affects.

values.label: Breathing rate at rest, adults
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.3 The Process of Breathing, Respiratory Rate and Control of Ventilation: “By adolescence, the normal respiratory rate is similar to that of adults, 12 to 18 breaths per minute.”
values.note: Reference only: the model holds breathing steady and does not speed it up or slow it down.

values.label: Tidal volume: air taken in by one quiet breath
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.3 The Process of Breathing, Respiratory Volumes and Capacities: “Tidal volume (TV) is the amount of air that normally enters the lungs during quiet breathing, which is about 500 milliliters.”
values.note: Reference only: the model works with shares of air, not volumes.

states.label: Supplemental oxygen
states.summary: Breathing air with a larger share of oxygen raises the oxygen pressure in every ventilated alveolus, so blood passing those alveoli loads more oxygen.
states.where: StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK482268, Alveolar Gas Equation, Introduction; Function: “PAO2 = [(Patm − PH2O) FiO2] − (PaCO2/RQ)” and “FiO2 is the fraction of inspired oxygen”
states.modelNote: The model raises the oxygen share of the air breathed in. It cannot add oxygen to blood that skips the air sacs: StatPearls NBK526127 notes that “true shunt does not improve with supplemental oxygen therapy.”

states.label: Narrowed airways to one region (for example an asthma attack)
states.summary: A narrowed airway lets less air reach the alveoli beyond it while their blood keeps flowing, so their oxygen pressure falls and their ventilation–perfusion ratio drops.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, Ventilation and Perfusion: “Ventilation is regulated by the diameter of the airways” and “In contrast, when ventilation is insufficient, the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli drops.” Ratio direction: “Ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs, and perfusion is the flow of blood in the pulmonary capillaries.”
states.modelNote: The model narrows the airway to its right-hand air sac.

states.label: Narrowed airways widened again
states.summary: When narrowed airways widen again, more air reaches the alveoli beyond them, so their oxygen pressure stays high and their ventilation–perfusion ratio rises back. Directions are compared with narrowed airways.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4 Gas Exchange, Ventilation and Perfusion: “Ventilation is regulated by the diameter of the airways” and “When ventilation is sufficient, oxygen enters the alveoli at a high rate, and the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli remains high.”
states.modelNote: The model starts from narrowed airways and opens them most of the way. Compare the readings with the narrowed-airways state, not with normal.

states.label: Pulmonary embolism (dead space)
states.summary: A clot blocks blood flow to part of the lung; those alveoli keep their air but lose their blood, so their ventilation–perfusion ratio rises toward dead space.
states.where: StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK526127, Respiratory Failure in Adults, Pathophysiology, Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch: “When ventilation is excessive to perfusion, the V/Q ratio is greater than one; Dead space ventilation occurs when the V/Q ratio reaches infinity.” and “Etiologies of V/Q mismatch include: Acute respiratory distress syndrome; Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; Congestive heart failure; Pulmonary embolism”. Alveolar gas directions from StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK539907, Mechanism: “In cases of high V/Q ratios, PO2 increases, and PCO2 decreases as alveolar air more closely matches the larger volume of inspired air than perfused blood.”
states.modelNote: The model blocks most of the blood to its right-hand air sac and sends that blood to the left-hand sac. The alveolar rows print air-weighted averages of both sacs.

states.label: Shunt: blood flowing past alveoli that get no air
states.summary: When alveoli get no air while blood keeps flowing past them, perfusion exceeds ventilation and the region's ventilation–perfusion ratio falls toward zero, a shunt.
states.where: StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK526127, Respiratory Failure in Adults, Pathophysiology, Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch: “When perfusion is excessive to ventilation, the V/Q ratio is less than one; Shunt occurs when the V/Q ratio reaches zero.” and “Unlike V/Q mismatch, true shunt does not improve with supplemental oxygen therapy.”
states.modelNote: The model takes the air away from most of its right-hand air sac by filling it with fluid; blood past that part becomes shunt. Other rows move in the model too, but the cited passages give a direction only for the region's ratio.
